extracted.intended_audience: educated public and correspondents (political leaders, scientists, editors, and friends)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of 18th‑century letters and essays offering normative guidance on public conduct, journalism, war, law of nations, taxation, and personal/professional decisions; useful as prescriptive principles for public correspondence and policy advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settle disputes by arbitration/peaceful means
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations should be induced and obliged to settle their disputes without cutting one another's throats; agree to settle differences by arbitration or even by chance (cast of a die) rather than by fighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin repeatedly insists that wars are ultimately misfortunes even to victors, and that the practice of settling disputes by violence is inferior to arbitration or other non‑violent resolution methods. He frames this as a moral and practical improvement in 'moral philosophy' that humanity ought to adopt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must refuse abusive personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: The conductor of a newspaper should consider himself the guardian of his country's reputation and refuse to insert writings that may hurt it; avoid publishing scandalous personal abuse commonly found in newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If people insist on printing their abuses, they should do so in pamphlets distributed where they please, not fill general newspapers with unprofitable and disagreeable matter. Editors owe subscribers distant from the scene not to stuff papers with such content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rash changes without seeing hidden costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make frequent, troublesome changes in life (or plans) because we feel present inconveniences and fail to see those that may exist elsewhere; rash changes often worsen matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the 'meadow turned marsh' anecdote: what looks pleasant at a distance may have unseen problems. Consider unseen disadvantages and weigh alternatives before acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections for noncombatants in war (law of nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In future wars, certain classes of persons and institutions should be protected and allowed to continue their employments safely: 1) cultivators of the earth; 2) fishermen; 3) merchants and traders in unarmed ships; 4) artists and mechanics in open towns; hospitals should be unmolested and assisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is to remove the lure of rapine from war by protecting those who produce for society; additionally, if goods (corn, fish, etc.) must be taken, the occupier should pay for them. This scheme is presented as a pragmatic and humane improvement to the law of nations to make peace more lasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish or relinquish privateering / stop legalized plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of privateering (state‑sanctioned plunder of commerce) is highly mischievous and should be voluntarily relinquished by powerful naval nations as an act of humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin argues that privateering makes the practice of plundering profitable and encourages piratical behaviour; powerful nations relinquishing the advantage would protect commerce and the innocent families of merchants, artisans, and cultivators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay for requisitioned goods during war
rubrics_metrics.description: If obliged to take corn, fish, or goods from farmers or others (friend or enemy), those who take them should pay for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment for taken supplies would remove encouragement to war that arises from rapine and make peace more likely to continue and be lasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duelling is unjustifiable and should be condemned
rubrics_metrics.description: Duelling is a murderous practice that decides nothing; it is unjustifiable to risk death over petty matters of 'honour'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally used when duels were thought to let Providence decide truth, modern duels settle nothing and are an absurd pride that makes individuals judge, condemn, and execute without jury. Franklin condemns the practice unequivocally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens must pay taxes and honor public obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Remissness or unwillingness to pay taxes (money justly due) is blameable; money due to creditors is no longer the people's money and should be collected by law if withheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin explains that most property (beyond natural necessities) is a creature of public convention and thus subject to public regulation; those who refuse the terms of civil society forgo its benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public right to regulate property for common welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: All property superfluous to the individual's natural needs is the property of the public (created by law) and may be disposed of by law whenever the public welfare requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a justification for taxation and regulation: civil society's benefits and protections imply powers of collective disposition for the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors should avoid stuffing papers with scandal and personal quarrels
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should not burden subscribers with unprofitable matter such as personal quarrels and abuses; a conductor ought to moderate content to avoid unjust or hurtful material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin gives a conversational example of quarrellers using abusive epithets and observes that spectators only learn that the two parties 'know one another'; newspapers should thus refrain from amplifying such disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When transcribing languages without orthography, note interpreter biases
rubrics_metrics.description: In languages without established orthography, different European interpreters will spell words according to the usual sounds in their own languages, so spellings may differ widely and hyphenation of syllables may be printer‑dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover pronunciation, one must know the usual powers of letters in the interpreter's language; compilers should be aware that spelling variations may reflect the transcriber's native orthographic habits (e.g., English, French, German).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer public works and industry over war expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Money spent in wars could have produced vast public utilities—agriculture improvements, canals, roads, bridges, aqueducts, and other works—that would increase comforts and conveniences for all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin uses this as a policy criterion: assess national priorities by comparing returns from war expenditure versus investment in public infrastructure and improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider age, health, and private affairs when holding public office
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials should assess whether their bodily strength and activity level remain adequate to public duties; infirmity, declining activity, and the burdens of office justify requesting discharge or replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin details how constant attendance and ministerial business can prevent the exercise and rest needed for health; he frames resignation as legitimate when public service would otherwise suffer due to personal decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value being a 'doer of good' above seeking reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher value should be placed on the character of a 'doer of good' than on other kinds of reputation; small writings that move one active mind in a hundred can have considerable effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin recounts how a book ('Essays to do Good') influenced his conduct lifelong; this supports prioritizing practical benevolence over fame or ostentation.
